title: The swipe happens before your point does: write a hook that earns three more seconds
markdown:
# The swipe happens before your point does: write a hook that earns three more seconds

The clip opened with the finished cake, a clean countertop, and the promise of a fast recipe. By the time the creator said what made it different, the viewer had already moved on. Nothing was wrong with the edit. The problem arrived earlier: the first frame gave people no reason to wait for the second.

For a short-form video, the opening is not a miniature introduction. It is a decision point. A viewer asks, usually without putting it into words: "Why should I stop here?" If the answer is generic, delayed, or buried under setup, the swipe wins.

This does not mean every video needs a shouted claim or a fake deadline. Those tricks can buy attention once and damage trust after that. A hook has a simpler job: make a specific promise that the video can keep.

## Start with the moment that changes the outcome

Creators often begin where the work began: "Today I'm going to show you..." That is useful context, but it makes the viewer wait for the payoff. Begin closer to the friction instead.

If the video teaches a repair, show the loose part and name the mistake that causes it. If it is a recipe, lead with the texture or shortcut people usually miss. If it is a product demo, show the failed task before the successful one. The opening should tell the viewer what is at stake and what they will get by staying.

Compare these two starts:

- "Here are three ways to improve your desk setup."
- "If your neck hurts at 3 p.m., your monitor may be the last thing to fix."

The second line gives the viewer a recognizable problem and creates a question the video can answer. It also narrows the audience. That is a feature. The people who do not have that problem were never the right viewers for this clip.

## Make one promise, then show proof quickly

A hook breaks when it promises a result that arrives too late. After the first line or visual, give the viewer evidence that the video knows what it is talking about: the before-and-after, the failed version, the relevant screen, or the result in motion.

That proof does not need to be polished. A close shot of a cracked zipper can do more work than a cinematic montage if the video is about fixing zippers. Specificity makes the claim believable because the viewer can see what the next seconds are for.

Keep the promise small enough to deliver. "Make every reel go viral" is not a promise anyone can trust. "Stop losing viewers before the tip starts" is a problem a short video can actually address.

## Write several openings before you choose one

The first hook that comes to mind usually sounds like the last five clips you watched. Give yourself alternatives. Write a direct problem, a surprising observation, a common mistake, and a visible result. Then read each one beside the first shot.

The words and image need to cooperate. A line about an expensive mistake paired with a calm talking head creates a mismatch. A clip that opens on the broken result, followed by a line that explains the cost of that result, gives the viewer a reason to stay.

Use this quick check before recording:

- Can someone understand the problem with the sound off?
- Does the opening make a claim the rest of the video can prove?
- Would the right viewer recognize themselves in the first sentence or frame?
- Does the next beat arrive before curiosity turns into impatience?

If an opening fails one of these, revise the opening rather than adding more editing later. Fast cuts cannot rescue a vague promise.

## Test the hook against the swipe

Watch the first three seconds with the rest of the video hidden. If the opening depends on later context, it is probably asking too much. Trim the greeting, move the best visual forward, and replace broad language with the detail that made you make the video in the first place.

This is also where honest hooks pull ahead of bait. A strong opening earns attention and then pays it back. If the video cannot answer the question it raises, the audience learns to leave earlier next time.

Hook-lab is built for this drafting step: turn a topic into multiple opening angles, pressure-test the promise, and choose a line that matches the footage you can actually deliver. Try it here: https://capafy.ai/agent/8123079349?ct=capafy-distribute-hook-lab

The goal is not to trap a viewer. It is to make the right person feel that the next few seconds are worth their time. When the first frame names a real problem and the video proves it can help, the swipe has less room to win.
